rationale: The Genesis worship-and-staff statement gives a concrete counterpart for this part of the Jacob account. The selected unit does not itself narrate both grandsons blessings; the separate blessing passage supplies that part.

Genesis narrates the hands placed over Josephs two sons and the blessing requesting blessing for the children. It supplies the blessing context beside the staff-worship comparison retained separately. Neither pair adds a second completion for this source.

Genesis records Joseph nearing death, promising Gods visitation and departure, and requiring his bones carried up. Those concrete clauses correspond to the exodus-and-bones summary; Hebrews adds by-faith interpretation.

Exodus gives the decree against male children and the mother seeing a beautiful child and hiding him three months. Hebrews speaks of parents and their lack of fear. Those additions are not made exact words of the Exodus narrative.

relationship: royal adoption and grown Moses brothers
rationale: Exodus narrates becoming Pharaohs daughters son and then grown Moses visiting his brothers under hard labor. Hebrews explicitly calls this a refusal by faith. The narrative is related without inventing a formal renunciation scene within the selected verses.

The preceding refusal of Pharaohs daughters son status supplies the action explained by this choosing-rather clause. Here the people-of-God mistreatment and temporary pleasure of sin give the contrast; those motives are not all printed in the preceding single unit.

The later exhortation to bear His reproach outside the camp supplies a concrete reproach counterpart to Christ-related reproach valued above Egypts treasures. The addressees action and Moses valuation are not treated as the same historical event.

relationship: not fearing the king in different cases
rationale: Both accounts explicitly deny fear of the king: the parents before the decree, and Moses at departure. Their actors, actions and the seeing-the-invisible description remain distinct. No unprinted identification of this departure with another fear narrative is required.

The Passover instructions name slaughter, blood on door parts and protection from the destroyer entering the houses. These provide concrete counterparts to Passover, sprinkled blood and the firstborn warning. The particular verbs and full instructions remain as printed.

relationship: Egyptian waters and Israel dry crossing
rationale: Exodus contrasts the returning waters over Egypts forces with Israel walking on dry ground amid the sea. Hebrews describes the crossing through faith and Egyptians being swallowed when attempting it. The narrative and interpretive summary retain their different forms.

relationship: Jericho days circuits and falling wall
rationale: Joshua narrates six days, the seventh days seven circuits and the wall falling after the shout. This supplies the concrete chronology and event beside Hebrews seven-day summary. Seven days and seven circuits on the last day are not exchanged.

Joshua narrates Rahab and her household being brought out and her preservation because she hid the messengers. Hebrews adds faith, receiving spies in peace and the contrast with disobedient people. The rescue details and faith summary remain distinct.

Acts names judges until Samuel the prophet, providing a specific counterpart for Samuel in this abbreviated list. It is not represented as naming every other listed person or supplying every exploit of the prophets.

Daniel reports righteousness found in him and God saving him from lions, which had not troubled him. This is a concrete lion-rescue counterpart to the righteousness and lion-mouth clauses. This supplied passage does not explicitly name an angel or closed mouths, and no whole anonymous group is identified.

relationship: fire unable to harm the faithful
rationale: Daniel names the angel with Azariah and companions, flame shaken out and fire not touching or troubling them. This gives a concrete fire-power counterpart. Hebrews does not name those actors or state that every sword, weakness and battle clause describes the same people.

relationship: child restored and returned to mother
rationale: The narrative of the child living and being given back to his mother supplies a specific instance beside women receiving their dead through resurrection. The other half of Hebrews unit concerns different tortured people and is compared separately.

The brother refuses during torture and expects the King of the world to raise those dying for His laws to everlasting renewal. This supplies specific torture-and-resurrection-hope correspondence. His release-from-present-life phrase describes death; it is not equated with Hebrews unaccepted release.

Acts narrates Paul and Silas being beaten and confined in prison with secured feet. These give concrete counterparts to flogging and imprisonment in the list. The target is not represented as explicitly naming every mockery or chain clause, or as identifying every anonymous sufferer.

The narrative of a prophetic rebuke followed by commanded stoning supplies a concrete example for that violence in the list. The reference does not identify an unnamed sawn-apart person or assert that the target narrates all the garments and other deaths here.

Elijahs cave scene and report of slain prophets and pursuit of his life supply a specific cave-and-persecution comparison. Hebrews gives a wider wandering list and the world-not-worthy judgment, which are not all printed in this narrative.

Both summarize the listed people as faithful while not receiving what was promised. Verse13 says promises and recalls dying and distant greeting; this says the promise and testimony through faith. The singular/plural and surrounding assertions remain without an added theory about every other promise.

The earlier law-perfected-nothing and better-hope statement supplies a concrete better/perfection comparison. Here God provides something better concerning us and perfection not apart from us. The scope, participants and exact statements retain their own wording.
